title: Chapter 90 — Heads or Tails
paragraphs: "De balena vero sufficit, si rex habeat caput, et regina caudam." — Bracton, l. 3, c. 3.

Latin from the books of the Laws of England, which taken with the context means that of all whales captured by anybody on the coast of that land, the King, as Honorary Grand Harpooner, must have the head, and the Queen be respectfully presented with the tail. A division which, in the whale, is much like halving an apple — there is no remainder. Now as this law, under a modified form, is to this day in force in England, and as it offers in various respects a strange anomaly touching the general law of Fast and Loose Fish, it is here treated in a separate chapter, on the same courteous principle that prompts the English railways to provide a separate car specially reserved for royalty. In the first place, as curious proof that the above-mentioned law is still in force, I proceed to lay before you something that happened within the last two years.

It seems that some honest sailors of Dover, or Sandwich, or some one of the Cinque Ports, had after a hard chase succeeded in killing and beaching a fine whale which they had originally spotted far off from the shore. Now the Cinque Ports are partially or somehow under the jurisdiction of a sort of policeman or official called a Lord Warden. Holding the office directly from the crown, I believe, all the royal revenues from the Cinque Port territories become his by assignment. Some writers call this office a sinecure. But not so. Because the Lord Warden is busily employed at times in pocketing his privileges — which are his chiefly by virtue of that same pocketing of them.

Now when these poor sun-burnt sailors, barefoot and with their trousers rolled high up on their weather-beaten legs, had wearily hauled their fat fish high and dry, promising themselves a good hundred and fifty pounds from the precious oil and bone — and in their imaginations already sipping fine tea with their wives and good ale with their friends, upon the strength of their respective shares — up steps a very learned and most Christian and charitable gentleman, with a copy of Blackstone under his arm. Laying it upon the whale's head, he says: "Hands off! This fish, my masters, is a Fast-Fish. I seize it as the Lord Warden's." Upon this, the poor sailors in their respectful consternation — so truly English — knowing not what to say, fell to vigorously scratching their heads all round, meanwhile ruefully glancing from the whale to the stranger. But that did nothing to mend the matter or soften the hard heart of the learned gentleman with his copy of Blackstone. At length one of them, after long scratching about for his ideas, made bold to speak:
"Please, sir, who is the Lord Warden?"
"The Duke."
"But the Duke had nothing to do with taking this fish?"
"It is his."
"We have been at great trouble and peril and some expense, and is all that to go to the Duke's benefit — we getting nothing at all for our pains but our blisters?"
"It is his."
"Is the Duke so very poor as to be forced to this desperate way of getting a livelihood?"
"It is his."
"I thought to relieve my old bed-ridden mother by part of my share of this whale."
"It is his."
"Won't the Duke be content with a quarter or a half?"
"It is his."

In a word, the whale was seized and sold, and his Grace the Duke of Wellington received the money. Thinking that viewed in certain lights the case might by a bare possibility in some small degree be deemed, under the circumstances, a rather hard one, an honest clergyman of the town respectfully addressed a note to his Grace, begging him to take the case of those unfortunate sailors into full consideration. To which the Duke in substance replied — both letters were published — that he had already done so, and received the money, and would be obliged to the reverend gentleman if in the future he would decline meddling with other people's business. Is this the still-militant old man, standing at the corners of the three kingdoms, on all hands demanding charity from beggars?

It will readily be seen that in this case the Duke's alleged right to the whale was a delegated one from the Sovereign. We must then inquire on what principle the Sovereign is originally invested with that right. The law itself has already been set forth. But Plowdon gives us the reason for it. Says Plowdon, the whale so caught belongs to the King and Queen "because of its superior excellence." And by the soundest commentators this has ever been held a compelling argument in such matters.
But why should the King have the head and the Queen the tail? A reason for that, you lawyers!

In his treatise on "Queen-Gold," or Queen's pin-money, an old King's Bench author, one William Prynne, writes thus: "The tail is the Queen's, that the Queen's wardrobe may be supplied with whalebone." Now this was written at a time when the black limber bone of the Greenland or right whale was widely used in ladies' corsets. But this same bone is not in the tail; it is in the head — which is a sad mistake for a learned lawyer like Prynne. But is the Queen a mermaid, to be presented with a tail? An allegorical meaning may lurk here.

There are two royal fish so styled by the English law writers: the whale and the sturgeon, both royal property under certain limitations, and nominally supplying the tenth branch of the crown's ordinary revenue. I know not that any other author has hinted at the matter, but by inference it seems to me that the sturgeon must be divided in the same way as the whale, the King receiving the highly dense and elastic head peculiar to that fish — which, symbolically considered, may possibly be humorously based on some presumed resemblance. And thus there seems a reason in all things, even in law.
